# Reading the Ghazal: Exile, Desire, and the Elusive Truth

The poem opens with a striking self-positioning: the speaker casts themselves as a refugee, someone perpetually seeking release, existing in a state of parole—neither fully free nor fully imprisoned. This liminal condition extends beyond the literal to the psychological and temporal. The speaker seems to be grappling with a former self that has been hidden, suppressed, or even erased, yet this reckoning does not happen in retrospect or through comfortable narrative distance. Instead, it unfolds in "real time," suggesting an urgency and rawness to this self-confrontation. The refugee here is not merely a political or physical exile but an exile from one's own history, forced to negotiate an identity that keeps shifting even as it is being examined.

This instability of self feeds directly into the ghazal's central preoccupation with longing and control. Classical ghazal form has always turned on the tension between desire and constraint, and this poem honors that tradition while complicating it. The recurring address to "Yaar"—a word that hovers between "friend" and "beloved"—becomes the site where questions of agency are staged. Who governs desire? Who leads, and who is led? The Yaar functions simultaneously as an intimate confidant and as a figure of authority, perhaps even fate itself, so that the poem's yearning is never simply romantic but shot through with an anxiety about who truly holds the reins of one's destiny.

Love, in this ghazal, cannot be separated from death. The imagery moves toward funerals and burned bodies, images that carry the weight of grief and irrevocable loss. This is not death as abstraction but death rendered in visceral, embodied terms—the charred remains standing in for the finality that love's failures or love's fulfillments equally seem to court. Crucially, the poem denies easy consolation. Even divine figures, even the smallest and most seemingly insignificant beings, find no comfort here. This refusal of solace elevates the poem's stakes: if not even the sacred or the humble can be soothed, then the grief being described is total, permeating every scale of existence.

Out of this atmosphere of loss emerges a troubling moral ambiguity. The poem places the terrorist and the victim in uncomfortably close proximity, refusing to let the reader settle into a clear moral hierarchy between them. Truth, the poem suggests, is not something that can be individually possessed or declared; it can only be approximated through collective testimony—what the poem calls being "polled." This democratic, almost bureaucratic image of truth-seeking stands in stark contrast to the intimate, lyrical mode of the ghazal itself, creating a productive friction between private feeling and public accountability.

The poem's closing turn is characteristically self-reflexive, a gesture common to the ghazal's final couplet, where the poet often signs their own name or comments on the act of composition itself. Here, the Beloved is revealed to have "stolen" the poet's very words, collapsing the distance between speaker and addressee, between the one who longs and the one who is longed for. This theft suggests that authorship itself is unstable, that the poem's meaning does not belong solely to its maker. The final lines gesture toward the future, insisting that clarity—about fate, about guilt, about love—will only arrive as the poem's "plot" continues to unfold, leaving the reader suspended in the same uncertainty that has animated the speaker throughout.

# The Immediacy of Suffering: Agha Shahid Ali's Ghazal "In Real Time"

Agha Shahid Ali, the Kashmiri-American poet celebrated for popularizing the ghazal form in English, crafted a particularly haunting example of this ancient Urdu poetic structure in his piece bearing the refrain "in real time." Written with an acknowledged debt to James Merrill—whose own formal innovations and preoccupations with mortality clearly influenced Ali's approach—and dedicated to poet Daniel Hall, this ghazal exemplifies how a strict traditional form can become a vessel for distinctly contemporary anxieties.

The ghazal form itself demands a peculiar kind of coherence-through-discontinuity: each couplet (or *sher*) must stand as an independent, self-contained unit, complete in itself, while still connecting to the whole through a shared refrain (*radif*) and rhyme scheme (*qafia*). This structural requirement for autonomy paradoxically creates unity, as the repeated phrase—here, "in real time"—acts as a kind of incantatory anchor, pulling seemingly unrelated images and moments into orbit around a central preoccupation.

What makes Ali's deployment of this refrain so powerful is its productive ambiguity. "In real time" evokes simultaneity, urgency, the unmediated present tense of catastrophe—but it also gestures toward broadcast media, toward the way violence and suffering are now witnessed as they happen, collapsing distance between event and audience. Throughout the poem, this phrase attaches itself to a startling range of material: bodies consumed by fire, acts of terrorism, the intimate rupture of a failed love affair, the desperate reaching of prayer toward a possibly absent God. These images don't develop narratively or argue a thesis; instead, they accumulate, each couplet offering its own self-contained crisis, its own moment of unbearable presence.

This elliptical, fragmented structure mirrors the poem's deeper concerns with exile and displacement—themes central to much of Ali's work, given his own biography as a Kashmiri Muslim living in America, witnessing political violence in his homeland from a geographic and temporal remove that the refrain "in real time" seems almost to protest against or long to collapse. The ghazal becomes a way of holding multiple registers of loss simultaneously: the personal (heartbreak, spiritual uncertainty) and the political (terrorism, bodies burning) refuse to remain separate, instead bleeding into one another through the insistent return of that phrase.

Crucially, the poem resists easy consumption. Its power doesn't announce itself on first reading but rather "unfolds"—to use language the summary itself employs—only through sustained, careful attention. This is perhaps fitting for a form whose couplets were traditionally meant to be savored individually, allowed to resonate before the reader moves to the next. Ali asks his readers to sit with disparate images of suffering, to let them accrue meaning slowly rather than resolving into tidy interpretation. The ghazal thus performs its own argument: that suffering, mortality, and doubt are not sequential problems to be solved but simultaneous conditions to be endured, witnessed, and—if we're patient enough—finally understood in their terrible, unified immediacy.

# The Pounding

James felt it before he understood it—a pounding that seemed to rise from somewhere beneath his ribs, insistent and unwilling to be ignored. It wasn't just his heartbeat, though that too had quickened. It was something deeper, a rhythm that matched the frantic churn of his thoughts.

He stood at the window, watching rain streak the glass, and tried to name what he felt. Anxiety, certainly. But underneath that, something else—anticipation, maybe, or the particular ache of waiting for news that would change everything. The pounding in his chest kept time with the pounding of the rain outside, as if the storm itself had crawled inside him and taken up residence.

James had always trusted his body to tell him things his mind refused to admit. When he felt this way—this pounding, insistent unease—it usually meant he already knew the answer to whatever question he was avoiding. He just hadn't let himself say it aloud yet.

The phone sat silent on the table behind him. He didn't turn to look at it. Instead, he pressed his palm flat against his sternum, feeling the pounding beneath his hand, feeling it feel him back, and thought: *whatever happens, I already felt this coming.*

Outside, the rain pounded harder. James closed his eyes and waited.

counterfactuals.output:
# Ghazal: In Real Time

*for Daniel Hall*

> "Time, the negative crystal..." —James Merrill

The dial tone breaks its silence, a small tide.
We speak across the wires in real time.

No archive holds the tremor of your voice—
each word arrives and dies in real time.

The old poets wrote to outlast their hour,
carved marble while the world moved in real time.

But you and I, dear friend, prefer the risk:
the unrehearsed line, spoken in real time.

Grief comes announced by nothing, no fanfare—
it enters as a guest, in real time.

I watched the syntax of your patience form
a shelter I could live in, real time.

Some love is architecture, built to last.
Some love is weather, changing in real time.

The page forgives revision; breath does not—
each sentence, once let go, was real, was time.

Sohrab, they say, the Yaar and the Beloved
are one voice split by distance, kept in time.

So, Shahid-hearted, let this ghazal close
the way all true talk does: in real time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

**Ghazal: In Real Time**

The anchors tally corpses as if sorrow streams in real time,
each numbered name a rumor drowned in dreams, in real time.

They've turned my mother's grief into a hashtag, a byline—
Srinagar trends for an hour, then it seems in real time.

The soldier at the checkpoint frames my exile with his camera,
uploads the curfew, likes multiply in schemes, in real time.

I dial the ruined valley; a voicemail full of static answers—
gunfire keeps better time than any hymn, in real time.

They say the martyrs' names dissolve like sugar into silence,
but I have tasted that sweetness char to phlegm in real time.

The postman never comes to the country I still call home—
only drones deliver what the government deems, in real time.

Each winter I unfold the shawl my grandmother once embroidered,
and grief unstitches every thread along its seam, in real time.

Call me Shahid—half elegy, half evidence, half hymn—
I sign this ghazal in the valley's blood-red gleam, in real time.

# Ghazal for Daniel Hall

The muezzin oversleeps; no call to chime in real time.
Even the faithful phone in late, past prime, in real time.

They hand the soldier back his name, changed like a crime—
his mother learns the news in perfect rhyme, in real time.

We begged the sky for reasons, any paradigm;
it answered with static, ash, the taste of lime, in real time.

I did not lose you to a bullet or a knife,
just to the calendar's slow, grinding mime, in real time.

Faith says wait, the dead lie past all crime—
but grief still weighs the evidence, tastes of grime, in real time.

not elegy, not prayer—just here, sublime, in real time.
